name: krukenberg tumour
aliases: metastatic signet-ring cell carcinoma of ovary

reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours; Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease
clinicalPearls: A Krukenberg tumour is a metastatic ovarian carcinoma characterised by mucin-filled signet-ring cells set in a cellular, often sarcomatoid-appearing ovarian stroma, and by definition is a secondary rather than a primary ovarian tumour.
The stomach is the commonest primary site, followed by the colon, appendix, breast and other gastrointestinal sources; the gallbladder, biliary tree and cervix are less frequent origins.
Ovarian involvement is bilateral in the large majority of cases, an important clue that an apparently ovarian mass is in fact metastatic.
It often affects women younger than those with primary ovarian carcinoma, and may occasionally present before the primary tumour is recognised.
The stroma can be hormonally active, producing oestrogen or androgen, so patients may present with abnormal uterine bleeding or virilisation in addition to a mass.

Immunohistochemistry helps confirm a gastrointestinal origin, with signet-ring cells typically expressing cytokeratin 20 and CDX2 and often being negative or only focally positive for cytokeratin 7 and characteristically negative for markers of primary ovarian epithelium.
Whenever bilateral solid ovarian masses with signet-ring morphology are found, a diligent search for an occult gastrointestinal or breast primary, including upper and lower endoscopy, is mandatory.
Management is directed at the underlying disseminated malignancy; oophorectomy is usually palliative and the overall outlook is poor.
reference.pathophysiology: The Krukenberg tumour represents metastatic spread to the ovary of a mucin-producing adenocarcinoma, most often gastric, in which malignant epithelial cells accumulate intracytoplasmic mucin that displaces the nucleus to give the signet-ring appearance. Metastasis is thought to occur predominantly by lymphatic and haematogenous routes, and possibly transcoelomic spread, which helps explain the frequent bilaterality and the involvement of ovaries even without gross peritoneal disease. A striking feature is the reactive proliferation of ovarian stroma around the infiltrating tumour cells; this stroma may undergo luteinisation and secrete steroid hormones, producing oestrogenic or androgenic effects. Because the ovary provides a hormonally responsive, vascular environment, it is a favoured site for such metastases, particularly in premenopausal women.

redFlags: bilateral solid ovarian masses, which strongly suggest metastatic rather than primary disease
signet-ring cell histology on ovarian sampling
new virilisation or abnormal uterine bleeding from hormonally active stroma
weight loss, dyspepsia or gastrointestinal bleeding pointing to a gastric or colonic primary
widespread peritoneal disease and ascites indicating advanced malignancy
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally poor because the tumour reflects disseminated metastatic carcinoma, and survival is measured in months for most patients, being influenced chiefly by the site, stage and treatability of the primary tumour.
pitfalls: Mistaking a Krukenberg tumour for a primary ovarian mucinous carcinoma and failing to search for the true primary.
Stopping the work-up after ovarian surgery without endoscopic evaluation of the stomach and bowel.
Overlooking a small or early gastric primary that may be clinically silent when the ovarian metastasis presents first.
Misattributing virilisation or bleeding to a primary sex-cord tumour rather than hormonally active metastatic stroma.
Assuming unilateral disease excludes a Krukenberg tumour, since a minority are unilateral.

management: Identify and stage the underlying primary first with endoscopy, imaging, and immunohistochemistry, since treatment is directed by the primary tumour type, not the ovarian metastasis
Treat as stage IV disease of the primary in essentially all cases, with systemic palliative intent as the default goal
Reserve curative intent for the rare case of a solitary resectable primary with isolated resectable ovarian disease and no other metastases, decided by a multidisciplinary tumour board
For a gastric or gastroesophageal primary use first line fluoropyrimidine and platinum based combination chemotherapy
Apply biomarker directed therapy where relevant to the primary, including HER2 and mismatch repair or microsatellite instability or PD-L1 status, to guide targeted or immune checkpoint therapy
Choose subsequent lines of therapy on progression using standard principles for metastatic disease from that primary, guided by performance status and organ function
Consider surgery on the ovaries as generally palliative, aimed at relieving pain, torsion, mass effect, bowel obstruction, or abnormal bleeding rather than cure
Time ovarian surgery to when the primary is characterised and, where feasible, its disease is being controlled
Pursue definitive surgery on the primary tumour using standard indications and resectability criteria for that primary, not altered simply by presence of the ovarian metastasis
Reserve radiotherapy for palliative symptom control such as pelvic pain or bleeding, since there is no established primary role for radiotherapy against the ovarian metastasis
Monitor with serial imaging and primary appropriate tumour markers, with CA125 sometimes followed given ovarian involvement
Track hormonally active stroma clinically, since change in abnormal bleeding or virilisation can reflect disease activity
Build ongoing surveillance for bowel obstruction, ascites, and venous thromboembolism into follow up
Refer promptly to a multidisciplinary team spanning upper gastrointestinal surgery, medical oncology, and gynaecological oncology, with early palliative and supportive care involvement
